name: lammps
why: Large-scale molecular dynamics simulator, real physics you can run at home on your own molecules and materials.

brief.what_it_is: LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator) is a classical molecular dynamics simulation code focused on materials modeling. You feed it an input script of commands describing atoms, interaction potentials, the simulation box and the run, and it prints progress to the screen and writes a logfile named log.lammps, plus whatever output files the script asks for. The docs describe it as open-source under GPLv2.
brief.why_it_exists: The docs say it was designed to run efficiently on parallel computers and to be easy to extend and modify. It was originally developed at Sandia National Laboratories, with most funding from the US Department of Energy, and now includes contributions from many groups.
brief.how_it_works: The executable reads commands from an input file (given with -in) or from standard input and runs the molecular dynamics steps they describe. Parallel runs are launched with mpirun or mpiexec, and the processors command controls how MPI tasks map onto the simulation box. Multi-threading per MPI task is set with the OMP_NUM_THREADS environment variable or the package command.

brief.install_notes: The brew formula provides lmp_mpi and lmp_serial. The docs point to several non-brew routes: static Linux x86_64 tarballs from download.lammps.org (no MPI, no python module), Debian/Ubuntu, Fedora, EPEL, OpenSuse, Gentoo and Arch AUR build scripts, plus a Conda route and CMake or make source builds. Optional packages such as KIM need extra steps. Using openkim.org potentials needs the openkim-models package or KIM-API download commands. I did not read the source-build pages, so the prerequisites are unverified.
brief.standout: It is a long-running, DOE-backed materials MD code that is extensible through its own styles and plugin mechanism and is available as a large set of prebuilt packages. Its docs are unusually thorough, with a full command reference and a list of benchmarks.
brief.status: Maintained as far as the docs show. The manual is stamped 30 Sep 2026 and the git info reads 30Sep2026, and the docs carry both stable and develop branch versions. I did not check the GitHub release or commit history directly.
brief.caveats: The static Linux binaries are not built for MPI. Several distro packages are maintained by third parties, and the LAMMPS developers say they have no control over those packages' timing or configuration. Some examples and accelerator features need optional packages compiled in. Parallel runs need the correct MPI launcher, and the redirection operator < may fail under mpirun. Floating-point round-off means trajectories can diverge across processor counts. The license is GPLv2. The homepage is the documentation site, not a project landing page, and it does not mention Homebrew.
quotes: LAMMPS is a classical molecular dynamics simulation code focusing on materials modeling.
It was designed to run efficiently on parallel computers and to be easy to extend and modify.
In theory you should get identical answers on any number of processors and on any machine.

judge.reason: LAMMPS lets you script classical molecular dynamics and explore how atoms and materials behave, making real scientific simulation an unusually hands-on rabbit hole.

entry.title: LAMMPS
entry.tldr: A molecular dynamics simulator from Sandia National Laboratories: write a script describing atoms and forces, and it steps the physics forward for you.
entry.deeper_look:
LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator) is a classical molecular dynamics code focused on materials modeling. You do not click through a GUI. You write an input script: commands that define the simulation box, place atoms, choose interaction potentials, and say how long to run. LAMMPS reads it, prints progress to the screen, and writes a logfile called log.lammps, plus any other output files the script asks for.

The docs say it was designed to run efficiently on parallel computers and to be easy to extend and modify. It was originally developed at Sandia National Laboratories, with most funding from the US Department of Energy, and now includes contributions from many groups. Extra force fields and behaviours are added through its own styles and a plugin mechanism.

The idea underneath is that a lot of materials science is Newton's laws applied to many atoms at once. You pick a model for how atoms push and pull on each other, then step forward in tiny increments of time and watch what emerges: melting, diffusion, fracture, flow. The same script can run on a laptop in serial or be spread across many processors with MPI. Small experiments make sense at home, and the manual is thorough enough to teach the vocabulary as you go.
entry.install:
brew install lammps
# installs lmp_serial and lmp_mpi. Parallel runs need an MPI launcher (open-mpi is pulled in as a dependency).

entry.whats_unique: It is a long-running, DOE-backed materials MD code that you extend with your own styles and plugins. Its documentation is unusually thorough, with a full command reference and benchmarks.
entry.caveats: You need to write or find an input script before anything happens, and some examples need optional packages that may not be compiled into the brew build.
